concepts: offline distillation of reasoning experience (vs. online reasoning from scratch)
contributions: Thinking with Reasoning Skills (TRS), a training-free, black-box-compatible framework that offline-distills both successful strategies and failure-mode fixes from long reasoning trajectories into compact, structured, retrievable skill cards, injected into a new query's prompt at inference time

empirical evidence that TRS breaks the efficiency-accuracy trade-off that budget-forcing methods (TALE, Chain-of-Draft) suffer on hard problems -- where enforced brevity causes catastrophic accuracy collapse -- by reducing redundant exploration through reused procedural guidance rather than forced conciseness

a controlled ablation showing the gains require both structured (not free-form) skill representation and sufficient library coverage, ruling out that TRS's benefit is merely from prepending relevant-looking context
demonstrated cross-model transferability of distilled skills (skills built from one model's trajectories improve a different target model), with transfer gains growing on harder problems
datasets: AoPS-derived contest-math library (7,616 problems) evaluated on AIME 2024/2025/2026 and HMMT
limitations: The paper's failure-case analysis is not yet as deep as its success-skill study: while TRS can distill 'failure-mode fixes' from incorrect trajectories, the current pipeline relies on limited supervision signals (final-answer correctness for math, pass/fail test-case information for coding), so which types of errors are most recoverable via skill distillation, and how to summarize fine-grained failure dynamics beyond these coarse signals, remain unstudied. TRS introduces an additional retrieval and prompt-injection layer whose end-to-end benefit depends on retrieval quality and controlling prompt inflation; in some settings (e.g. when completion tokens do not decrease or prompts grow too long, as seen for GPT-OSS-120B on coding) cost may not strictly improve even if accuracy does. Evaluation is currently bounded to math and competitive programming with automatic verifiers; broader domains, weakly verifiable tasks, and open-ended workflows remain future work. A large design space is left open: which model should generate the original CoT to summarize, how to choose or ablate the summarizer more systematically, how to compress many problem-level skills into fewer general skills, and how retrieval design should scale as the skill library grows very large.
method: TRS decouples acquiring reasoning logic from executing it. Offline Skill Library Construction: for each source training instance, run the reasoning model to get a trajectory and correctness verdict, then distill the (question, trace, verdict) record with a stronger summarizer model (Gemini 3 Flash) into a compact, structured skill card with five fields (Trigger/Do/Avoid/Check/Risk) plus 10-20 retrieval-trigger keywords -- if the trajectory succeeded, the card captures the essential solution pattern (invariant, algorithmic template); if it failed, the card captures a reusable anti-pattern-to-correction fix. Cards are validated for abstraction (no copied instance-specific constants/answers), actionability (executable steps), and compactness, and stored as key-value entries in a retrievable library, indexed by BM25 (default for math), dense BGE-M3+FAISS embeddings, or hybrid retrieval (default for coding). Online Retrieval and Skill Injection: for a new query, retrieve the top-k most relevant skill cards (even without a near-duplicate problem existing) and prepend them to the prompt with a lightweight arbitration instruction ('use only directly applicable skills; ignore irrelevant or contradictory advice'), guiding the model toward an effective solution path while keeping intermediate reasoning concise. Evaluated on DeepMath-103K (93K for library construction, 10K held out) and Nemotron-Competitive-Programming-v1 (26.6K filtered training instances, 1K held-out), across GPT-OSS-120B, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, GPT-4o-mini, and Doubao Seed (1.8 Pro for math, 2.0 Pro for coding), against Direct reasoning-from-scratch, TALE-EP (budget-constrained prompting), Chain-of-Draft (brevity-constrained), and NoWait (reflection-marker suppression) baselines, sliced by baseline-model thinking-token difficulty thresholds to isolate hard instances.
one_liner: Thinking with Reasoning Skills (TRS) is a training-free, black-box-compatible framework that offline-distills long deliberation trajectories (successes and failures) into compact, retrievable 'skill cards' (Trigger/Do/Avoid/Check/Risk), retrieves and injects the most relevant cards into a new query's prompt at inference time instead of forcing the model to re-derive solution logic from scratch, and empirically reduces reasoning tokens while matching or improving accuracy versus standard CoT across multiple LLMs on math and coding benchmarks -- with gains growing on harder problems, unlike budget-forcing baselines (TALE, Chain-of-Draft) which collapse below baseline accuracy as difficulty increases.
problem: Reasoning LLMs spend substantial tokens on long intermediate reasoning traces containing redundant verification and trial-and-error loops, but existing token-efficient reasoning methods (compressing traces via minimalist drafts like Chain-of-Draft, enforcing explicit token budgets like TALE, or suppressing reflection markers like NoWait) still treat every query as a blank slate -- the model re-derives solution logic from scratch, just faster -- which forces the model to skip crucial steps and fail on hard problems when the reasoning space is compressed too aggressively.

relevance.overthinking: Directly central to the topic and explicitly framed as an efficient-reasoning method addressing the same production-scale token/cost problem the literature studies: its headline empirical claim is that efficiency need not come at the expense of correctness if a model reuses distilled experience rather than merely being forced to be brief. The paper's key contrast with budget-forcing/brevity-enforcing baselines (TALE, Chain-of-Draft) -- which it shows collapse in accuracy on hard problems precisely because they compress the reasoning space rather than removing genuinely redundant exploration -- is a direct, benchmarked counterexample to a common overthinking-mitigation strategy, and its difficulty-sliced accuracy curves are a clean empirical demonstration of exactly the accuracy-cliff failure mode that naive length-penalty approaches to overthinking risk.

results: On math, TRS reduces completion tokens/cost while preserving or improving accuracy across all four models: Gemini-3-Flash +0.7pp accuracy with 17.5% cost reduction, GPT-4o-mini +1.8pp with 20.6% cost reduction, Doubao Seed -0.2pp accuracy with 53.8% cost reduction, GPT-OSS-120B accuracy preserved (+/-0%) with 16.9% cost reduction. On coding, TRS generally improves pass@1 with lower cost: GPT-4o-mini +2.4pp with 6.3% cost reduction, Doubao Seed +0.8pp with 6.0% cost reduction, GPT-OSS-120B +4.1pp though cost slightly increases (+4.8%) due to larger prompts. Difficulty-sliced analysis (Figure 4) is the paper's central result: as baseline thinking-token threshold theta increases (harder instances), TALE and Chain-of-Draft show catastrophic accuracy collapse (e.g. dropping below baseline on GPT-OSS for theta>10k), while TRS consistently matches or exceeds baseline accuracy, achieving ~45-80% relative uplift on the hardest GPT-OSS tasks -- retrieved skills act as a 'navigation map' preventing the model from getting lost in incorrect branches, rather than forcing brevity that cripples deep reasoning. On Doubao, TRS achieves the lowest token consumption among all methods, cutting generated tokens for hard problems (theta>=12k) from ~12k to ~5k while maintaining top accuracy; on GPT-OSS it roughly halves token usage (~15k to ~7k) without the accuracy loss seen in budget-forcing 'speed-limit' approaches. A controlled representation/coverage ablation (fixed 500-question DeepMath subset) shows naive retrieval alone does not explain the gains: raw examples, raw CoT traces, free-form summaries, and small structured-card libraries (2.5k cards) all underperform the full TRS library (93k cards), with the strongest result appearing only when structured skill reuse is paired with sufficient library coverage -- confirming TRS retrieves reusable procedural guidance, not merely relevant-looking context. Cross-model skill transfer (Doubao-derived and OSS-derived libraries applied to the other model) shows transfer gains grow with problem difficulty and skills are broadly transferable across models, though same-source skills (e.g. a Doubao library used on Doubao) generally yield the highest accuracy due to stylistic alignment. External transfer to a separate AoPS-derived contest-math library (7,616 cards) on 120 held-out AIME-style questions shows a heterogeneous but net-positive pattern: 13 of 25 model-benchmark pairs improve accuracy and 20 of 25 reduce per-query cost, with Doubao-1.8 the clearest average beneficiary (+1.88 accuracy points, 2.8% cost reduction).
